The present work is devoted to the study of the Zr 4 þ /Ti 4 substitution in the K1/2 Bi1/2 Ti(1x )Zr x O3 solid solution ( x ¼ 0.0 to x ¼ 1.0), based upon the K1/2Bi1/2TiO3 (KBT) ferroelectric compound. The tetragonal distortion of KBT is suppressed by this substitution and leads to the cubic compound K1/2Bi1/2ZrO3 (KBZ). These results agree with the values of the ionic radii of the Zr 4 þ and Ti 4 ions ( r Ti 4 þ ¼ 0.605 A ˚ and r Zr 4 þ ¼ 0.72 A ˚ ). Close to KBT ( x /C20 0.05), the symmetry remains tetragonal. For higher values of x , the '' a '' lattice parameter (cubic indexing) follows Vegard's law, thus confirming the formation of a solid solution. The transformation from tetragonal to cubic proceeds via an intermediate pseudocubic symmetry (0.1 /C20 x < 0.5), for which the X-ray diffraction peaks present small broadening and asymmetry. For x /C21 0.5 and up to the KBZ compound ( a /C25 4.158 A ˚ ), the samples are cubic but some extra peaks are also observed, indicating the occurrence of a secondary phase. The microstructure shows fine-grained ceramic samples for the first range, while for the KBZ-rich range the grains are micrometer-sized and associated to very small grains of the secondary phase. Piezoelectricity is observed for the tetragonal and pseudocubic range, the substitution quickly reducing the piezoelectric properties. The measurement of the dielectric properties revealed close to KBT a dielectric anomaly probably associated to the tetragonal-cubic phase transition. For thepseudocubic and cubic range, a broad dielectric anomaly is observed around 300 8 C, corresponding to a relaxor behavior.

1 Introduction The perovskite compounds ABO3 are one of the most common oxide structures. Thus, they have been extensively studied, since they present a very large panel of interesting physical properties such as ferroelectricity and piezoelectricity [1-8], superconductivity [9-11], giant magneto-resistance [12-14]. The interest for such compounds was recently renewed since multiferroic properties were evidenced in such materials [15-17], as well as new peculiar ferroelectric properties at the nanoscale [18, 19] or for thin-film form [20] and new physical phenomena due to interface properties [21-23]. Concerning the piezoelectric properties, the industrially used compounds mainly belong
modulated by binary or ternary solid-solution formation, such as NBT-KBT [33-35], NBT-BaTiO3 [36], NBTKBT-BaTiO3 [37], NBT-KBT-Li0.5Bi0.5TiO3 [38, 39], NBT-SrTiO3 [40, 41], double substitutions like for NBT-PbZrO3 [42], NBT-BiScO3 [42], NBT-BiFeO3 [42-44], NBT-KBT-BiAlO3 [45] or more comple x substitution on A-sites [46]. Some of these substitutions improve the piezoelectric properties of NBT and KBT, while some of them suppress the ferroelectricity, inducing sometimes interesting dielectric properties and/or relaxor behavior. Thus, as for the PZT, the understanding of the relationships between structure and electrical properties is necessary, in order to be able to modulate and control the properties of the compounds before using them in devices.
At the present time, most of the studies concern the substitutions in the A-site of the perovskite lattice. But up to date, very few studies concern the substitution on B-sites alone. As for PZT, Zr 4 þ ions would logically replace Ti 4 þ on B-sites. In order to test for this substitution, we selected the compound K1/2Bi1/2TiO3 (KBT), a ferroelectric compound [10] of tetragonal symmetry (space group P4mm [ a ¼ 3.994 A ˚ , c ¼ 4.038 A ˚ [47, 48]). The tolerance factor of KBT is larger than one ( t /C25 1.03) and thus implies structural distortion by displacement of cations, like in BaTiO3 ( t /C25 1.06) and PbTiO3 ( t /C25 1.02), a lone-pair effect being observed in the last one (like for Bi 3 þ ion). As the ionic radius of the Zr 4 þ ion is larger than that of Ti 4 þ ( r Ti 4 þ ¼ 0.605 A ˚ and r Zr 4 þ ¼ 0.72 A ˚ for coordination number ¼ 6 [49]), this structural distortion will decrease when substituting Zr 4 þ for Ti 4 þ . For the hypothetical compound K1/2Bi1/2ZrO3 (KBZ), the calculated tolerance factor is smaller than unity ( t /C25 0.97), thus similar to that of BaZrO3 ( t /C25 1.00, cubic, space group Pm3m) and of PbZrO3 ( t /C25 0.96, orthorhombic, space group Pbam). Thus, a modification of structural distortion type can be predicted for the K 1/2 Bi1/2 Ti(1x )Zr x O3 solid solution, the change probably occurring around x /C25 0.5 ( t /C25 1). Furthermore, this substitution will also suppress the polar (ferroelectric) behavior of KBT: a tolerance factor smaller than unity generally implies structural distortions by octahedra rotations, which are unfavorable to ferroelectricity, but lead more to antiferroelectric behavior. Moreover, (i) the calculated tolerance factor lies between those of BaZrO3 (paraelectric) and PbZrO3 (antiferroelectric), and (ii) Pb 2 þ and (K þ /Bi 3 þ ) pseudoion present similar ionic radii and lone-pair effect ( r Pb 2 þ ¼ 1.49 A ˚ and r K þ = Bi 3 þ ¼ 1.51 A ˚ for coordination number ¼ 12 [49]).
At the present time, very few data are available for the KBZ compound or the KBT-KBZ solid solution. Smolenski et al. [50] reported in 1967 for the possible existence of KBZ. A cubic-like X-ray diffraction pattern was published in 1985 [51] and a JCPDS/PDF card based upon this report was assigned to this compound [52]. But considering the tolerance factor calculated for KBZ, the real structure probably corresponds to distortion by octahedron tilting and thus to a noncubic unit cell [53]. Concerning the K1/2Bi1/2Ti(1x )Zr x O3 system (KBT-KBZ), a continuous solid-solution was reported in a short study mainly dedicated to the dielectric properties [54]. A symmetry change from tetragonal to rhomboedral was also reported for x /C25 0.1, with a very small rhomboedral distortion ( d r < 10 min angle).
Thus, the published results are ambiguous concerning both the hypothetical KBZ compound and the KBT-KBZ solid solution. As a consequence, the aim of the present study is: (i) to confirm for the possibility of the Zr/Ti substitution in the K1/2Bi1/2Ti(1x )Zr x O3 solid solution. (ii) to verify the existence of the K1/2Bi1/2ZrO3 compound and (iii) to measure the dielectric and piezoelectric properties of such materials.
2 Experimental procedure All the samples were elaborated by solid-state reaction using ZrO2 (SigmaAldrich 99.99%), TiO2 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.8%), KNO3 (Ventron > 99%) and Bi2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.9%). The ZrO2 and TiO2 raw materials were first separately ball milled in ethanol for 2 h at 390-400 rpm using agate balls in an agate container (planetary mill ''pulverisette'', Fritsch, IdarOberstein, Germany), in order to reduce their mean particle sizes. They were then dried at 200 8 Cinorder to suppress any residual water. After drying, these precursors were weighed according to the desired composition and homogenized by ball milling in ethanol for 2 h at 390-400 rpm. The obtained powders were then calcined at 900 8 C for 4 h, milled again and annealed between 900 and 1000 8 C for 4 h ( x ¼ 0.4 to x ¼ 1), while this second calcination was performed for 10 h for the Ti rich range ( x ¼ 0 to x ¼ 0.3). In order to determine the best calcination temperatures, simultaneous thermogravimetric and differential thermal analysis (TG/DSC Netzsch STA 409, Selb, Germany) was performed on the initial mi x of raw powders for different compositions, using a 10 8 C/min heating rate. After calcination, the obtained powders were studied by X-ray diffraction (Bruker D8, u /2 u configuration, LinxEye high-speed detector, CuK a 1 radiation, step size 0.08 8 , Bruker AXS, Karlsruhe, Germany). The powders were then pressed into 10 mm diameter disks ( /C25 43 MPa) and sintered at 1000-1070 8 C for 1 h. The obtained pellets were then electroded using platinum paint sintered at 800 8 C for half an hour. The electrical characterizations were performed on these pellets using an impedance analyzer (HP 4194A, Agilent technologies, Santa Clara, California, USA) at several frequencies between 100 Hz and 1 MHz. The piezoelectric properties were evaluated, after a poling process. This one was carried out in a silicone oil bath at room temperature using a 10 kV DC high-voltage source (SL10, Spellman, New York, USA). The piezoelectric constant d 33 was measured using a piezo-d33 meter (PM 300, Piezotest, London, UK). Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, JEOL JSM-7400F) was employed for microstructural characterization on fractured samples coated with carbon. The average grain size was determined for grains presenting suitable contrast by using image processing. For each sample, More than 50 grains were selected and used for the calculation of equivalent diameters.

3.1 Thermal analysis of the precursors In order to determine the best calcination temperatures, simultaneous TG/DSC measurement was performed on the initial mix of rawpowderscorresponding to the KBT composition (Fig. 1). Similar results were obtained for compositions containing zirconium. Four endothermic events were evidenced by DTA. The first one corresponds to the polymorphic transformation a KNO3 $ b KNO3 (128 8 C) and the second one to the melting of KNO3 (334 8 C) [55]. The third event, quite large and diffuse, is associated to the progressive decomposition of liquid KNO3. The last event corresponds to the transformation a Bi2O3 ! d Bi2O3, which occurs at /C25 730 8 C [56]. Thus, the reaction between the different precursors implies a liquid phase. The measured weight loss (11%) corresponds well to the calculated one (10.9%) and are totally achieved above 800 8 C. Thus, we selected 900 8 C for the synthesis of the samples.
3.2 X-ray diffraction The structural evolution was studied after calcinations of the powders, for compositions ranging from x ¼ 0.0 to x ¼ 1.0 (Fig. 2). Whatever the composition, the main peaks of the pseudocubic cell are shifted to lower angles with KBZ substitution, indicating an increase of the mean pseudocubic lattice parameter, and thus the formation of a solid-solution. Contrary to a previous report [54], we did not observe any evidence for rhomboedral symmetry for x > 0.1.
3.2.1 The KBT-rich-range For the KBT-rich range (0.0 < x /C20 0.4), all the diffraction peaks are broad, which implies a chemical disorder. The diffraction patterns appear quite complicated (Fig. 2). The (111) pseudocubic peak is splitted into two peaks (labelled A and B, Fig. 2b) and the angular position of these two peaks remains quasi-constant from x ¼ 0.05 to x ¼ 0.2. The (200) pseudocubic peak is split into two or three peaks (labelled C and D, Fig. 2b). Again, the angular position of these peaks remains quasi-constant from x ¼ 0.05 to x ¼ 0.2. All these peaks can be attributed to two different perovskite structures P1 and P2, corresponding,

The intensities of the peaks corresponding to perovskite P1 and P2 changes in reverse order, indicating that the content in P1 increase with x values, while P2 content decreases. Considering the angular position on the corresponding peaks and thus the mean pseudocubic lattice parameter, P1 and P2 have different Zr/Ti ratio, P2 containing less zirconium than P1. The same phenomena are also observed for the other peaks of the perovskite structure in the same composition range.

Thus, the X-ray diffraction patterns for powders calcined at low temperatures (900-1400 8 C) corresponds to the occurrence of two perovskite phases with different lattice parameters, as observed for our samples.
For the KBT-KBZ, the corresponding powders (0.0 /C20 x /C20 0.4) appear similarly as being out of equilibrium: the chemical reaction between the different precursors is not fully achieved. As a consequence, we tried to complete the chemical reaction by performing annealing of the powders. For example, the X-ray diffraction diagrams of the x ¼ 0.10 composition obtained for different annealing times is represented in Fig. 3 (samples from the same initial batch: onestar for the first sample successively annealed three times for 10 h, two stars is for the second sample directly annealed for 50 h twice). The results clearly demonstrate a structural evolution (Fig. 3b): the ''cubic'' phase, associated to the most intense (200) peak progressively disappeared, while the (002) and (200) tetragonal peaks merged into a single (200) pseudocubic peak. This evolution corresponds to the chemical homogenization of the sample and can be explained by considering that the powder is initially composed of two perovskite structures with different chemical compositions (different Ti/Zr ratio), which evolves

For x ¼ 0.05, the final symmetry was determined as being tetragonal with very small distortion. For the other compositions, the final symmetry appeared as pseudocubic, the departure from cubic symmetry appearing only as an asymmetry of the diffraction peaks (Fig. 4b). As we will see below, this departure from ''pure'' cubic symmetry can explain the piezoelectric properties observed for these compositions.
As Bi-containing compounds such as NBT and KBT are prone to loss of volatile elements (Bi, Na, K) and as long dwell times at temperatures up to 1000 8 C could imply volatilization, the powders were systematically weighed before and after annealing. Under the sensitivity of these measurements, no weight loss was observed. However, a small deviation from nominal composition cannot be excluded, which could explain the occurrence of secondary phases for long annealing times.

Only small differences are observed compared to the JCDS card [52]: (i) the (100) peak is observed here, while it was not reported and (ii) some of the intensities present small differences for high Miller indices. These peaks were also observed, with lower intensity, for the samples corresponding to 0.4 /C20 x /C20 1. Some of them could be assigned to monoclinic ZrO2, one of our precursors, but all of them could not be totally attributed. This difference in sizes and grain shapes suggests a modification of the sintering mechanism for KBZ-rich samples, the zirconium substitution inducing faster grain growth and thus increased porosity.
In addition, an intergranular phase is also observed, particularly for the KBZ-rich range, with very small grain size around 10-20 nm. This phase can be probably attributed to the unidentified secondary phase observed for these compositions by X-ray diffraction.
As a structural evolution occurred during annealing of some of the initial powders, we suspected that a similar phenomenon could occur during sintering. Thus, some of the samples were checked by X-ray diffraction ( x ¼ 0.5, x ¼ 0.8 and x ¼ 1.0). No difference was detected in the X-ray diffraction patterns before and after sintering.
3.3.2 Piezoelectric properties The poling process was performed for all the samples. Poled ceramics were obtained for 0 /C20 x /C20 0.4 using E /C25 3.5-4 kV/mm for x ¼ 0 (coercive field of KBT is reported as 3.5 kV/mm [61]), and E /C25 2 kV/mm for the others samples. Attempts to increase the applied field did not increase the measured d 33 value. But, we did not succeed in poling any of the other samples (electrical breakdown occurred). The measurement of the ferroelectric cycles was also unsuccessful because of high conductivity, even for the samples that appeared as being piezoelectric after poling.
According to the structural observations indicating a tetragonally distorted structure for x ¼ 0.05 and a pseudocubic structure for x ¼ 0.1 to x ¼ 0.4, the piezoelectric coefficient d 33 (Fig. 9) rapidly decreases with increasing x values, up to 2.4 pC/N for x ¼ 0.1, then remains quasiconstant up to x ¼ 0.3 and vanishes for x ¼ 0.4 ( d 33 ¼ 0.3 pC/N, i.e. lower than the instrumental error estimated to /C6 1 pC/N). These results agree well with the structural evolution determined by X-ray diffraction: like KBT, the x ¼ 0.05 sample is tetragonal (with very small distortion), thus piezoelectric. For 0.1 /C20 x /C20 0.4, the samples appears as pseudocubic, the departure from pure cubic

symmetry appearing only as an asymmetry of the diffraction peaks. Since these samples are not purely cubic, obtaining piezoelectricity is not surprising.
However, the piezoelectric constant values obtained for x ¼ 0.1 to x ¼ 0.4 are small, ( d 33 ¼ 2.4 pC/N for x ¼ 0.1 and d 33 ¼ 0.3 pC/N for x ¼ 0.4). Finally, obtaining piezoelectricity for x ¼ 0.4, but with a very small piezoelectric response, confirms that this composition is not truly cubic, even if we did not detect obvious structural distortion by X-ray diffraction. This fact also indicates that for higher values of x , the piezoelectric properties are suppressed by the substitution and that the corresponding compositions are centrosymmetric, as observed by X-ray diffraction.
3.3.3 Dielectric properties The relative permittivity and dielectric losses were measured as a function of temperature and frequency for some of the samples (Figs. 10 and 11). The analysis of the electrical properties must take into account the low densities of some of the samples, since dielectric measurements generally require density values over 95%. Indeed, some of the samples present densities lower than 90%.
The values of tan( d ) are high and increase quickly above 300 8 C, indicating high conductivity. Thus, the apparent increase of permittivity above 400-500 8 C (especially for low frequencies) is correlated to conductivity. Generally, high conductivity for dielectric materials can have two different origins: (i) a lack of densification, (ii) a microstructural effect and (iii) the occurrence of structural defects like vacancies. For the KBT-rich range of this solid solution, the densification is over 95%. Thus, the origin of conductivity here must be more related with the occurrence of vacancies. Indeed, potassium and bismuth are known as being volatiles and losses of such chemical elements during sintering would create defects. For the KBZ-rich range, which presents low densification, such conductivity phenomena are probably much more correlated with the lack of densification.

Concerning the relative permittivity and as for previously published results [54], a broad anomaly is observed, with a maximum around /C25 300 8 C, which is higher than previously reported for this system (150-200 8 C).
This maximum can be attributed to the tetragonal-cubic phase transition only close to KBT, since the x ¼ 0.05 sample appears as tetragonal, but the other compositions present a pseudocubic symmetry up to x ¼ 0.4 and a through cubic symmetry for 0.5 /C20 x /C20 1. In addition, this anomaly is frequency dependent (see tan( d ) curves) and thus clearly associated to a relaxor behavior.
Indeed, such behavior is characterized by the occurrence of a very broad e ( T ) peak (or e 0 ( T ) in comple x notation of relative permittivity) and a strong frequency dispersion in the peak temperature ( T m) and in the magnitude of e 0 below T m [62]. This anomaly can also be observed in the tan( d ) (or e 00 ) curves, the temperature for the maximum in e 0 appearing always higher than in e 00 (or tan( d )) curves. The absence of an obvious phase transition associated to these anomalies is also generally one of the representative features of relaxor materials [63].
As is well known for the ''model'' relaxor, PbMg1/3 Nb2/3O3 (PMN), such behavior is due to the occurrence of polar nanoregions (PNRs), which induces random-site electric dipoles, and the breadth of the e 0 ( T ) peak is a manifestation of the dipolar glass-like response of these materials [62]. If the relaxor nature of NBT and KBT materials is known for a long time and widely accepted, their origin was still controversial up to recent times. Indeed, NBT presents a long-range ferroelectric order at room temperature, but at the so-called depolarization temperature ( T d /C25 220 8 C), relaxor behavior was observed, together with a broad maximum in the e ( T ) curve around /C25 300 8 C, and an apparently antiferroelectric behavior between these two temperatures. Recent studies have clearly demonstrated for NBT, and thus probably also for KBT, that the dielectric anomalies have their origin in the occurrence of PNRs: The peculiar temperature T d of NBT (and thus also for KBT), where the ferroelectric order disappears, is the temperature for which long-range ferroelectric order reverts back to the relaxor state upon heating [64]. The behavior of these materials is thus clearly of relaxor type, with a long-range ferroelectric order established at room temperature for NBT and KBT.
As for other comple x perovskite materials, the occurrence of a relaxor behavior for the KBT-KBZ solid solution is thus not surprising and can be considered as a consequence of the mixed occupation of A- and B-sites [65]. Indeed, for NBT and KBT, A-sites are occupied both by Bi 3 þ and by an alkaline ion (Na þ , K þ ). The mixed A-site occupation is thus responsible for their relaxor behavior.
In addition, a ferroelectric/relaxor crossover can also be observed when compositional disorder is introduced by chemical substitutions [66] in ferroelectric materials, the behavior changing from 'pure'' ferroelectric to ''pure'' relaxor behavior. Such phenomena have been observed for example for BaTiO3-BaZrO3-CaTiO3 system, for which

abstract: Doping of suitable metal ions in ferroelectric oxides modifies the physical properties and can induce additional functionalities. Here, we present a detailed study on the effects of Sm concentration on the structural, dielectric, ferroelectric, and piezoelectric properties of ((K 0.5 Na0.5 ) 1 -3 x Sm x )NbO3 (KNSN) (0.00 ≤ x ≤ 0.02) ceramics. X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopic analysis indicate that KNSN ceramics exhibit the single-phase orthorhombic ( Amm 2) structure for x = 0.00 and the coexistence of orthorhombic and tetragonal ( Amm 2 + P 4 mm ) structure for the composition range 0.005 ≤ x ≤ 0.02. The tetragonal phase fraction increases with an increase in Sm concentration. We observed dielectric relaxation behavior in KNSN at orthorhombic to tetragonal ( T O-T ) phase transition temperature, and its origin can be attributed to the structural heterogeneity at the inter-ferroelectric phase boundary. Increasing Sm concentration leads to the broadening of the ferroelectric phase transition peaks. Further, the structural heterogeneity of the ceramics was seen from the slope of the dielectric constant versus log frequency and central peak behavior of Raman spectra at room temperature (RT). introduction:
Ferroelectric and piezoelectric materials belonging to perovskite structure show the highest piezoelectric coefficients and strong electromechanical coupling and, hence, are widely used for various device applications, such as sensors, actuators, capacitors, transducers, underwater acoustics, and ultrasonic medical imaging. 1,2 Among the plethora of ferroelectric materials, the lead (Pb)based ferroelectric perovskites, such as Pb(Zr x Ti 1 -x )O3 (PZT), (1 -x )Pb(Mg1/3 Nb 2/3 O 3 )x PbTiO3 (PMNx PT), are primarily used in various electronic devices due to their excellent dielectric, ferroelectric, and piezoelectric properties. 1-6 However, the high lead content ( > 60 wt%) in these ferroelectric perovskites causes serious concern due to lead toxicity. 4,6 The release of poisonous Pb into the atmosphere cannot be avoided during the hightemperature synthesis due to its high vapor pressure. 2 To increase the awareness of environmental safety worldwide, restrictions on using hazardous Pb-based material systems in various electronic devices were imposed by directives on 'Waste of Electrical and Electronic Equipment' and 'Restriction of certain Hazardous Substances.' 4,5,7,8 Hence, alternatives to lead-based materials in various electronic devices are needed, and research and development are now concentrated on eco-friendly and environmentally benign materials. Various lead-free ferroelectric systems, such as BaTiO3 (BT), (Na0.5 Bi 0.5 )TiO3 (NBT), (K0.5 Bi 0.5 )TiO3 (KBT), and (K0.5 Na 0.5 )NbO 3 (KNN), are widely studied by different research groups around the globe. 2-13 Among those ferroelectric systems, alkali niobate-based KNN ceramics have received significant attention since 2003 after the famous work in textured (Li, Ta, and Sb) modified KNN ceramic by Saito et al. 14
KNN is ferroelectric material with a high Curie temperature ( T C ∼ 420 ◦ C), a moderate piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 = 80 pC/N), high remanent polarization ( P r = 33 µ C/cm 2 ), and a high coercive field (20 kV/cm). 7,15 At room temperature (RT), KNN crystallizes into an orthorhombic crystal structure with the space group (SG) Amm 2. 7,16,17 Similar to BaTiO 3 , the KNN system undergoes a sequence of phase transitions as a function of temperature. With increasing temperature, KNN transforms from

The moderate piezoelectric coefficient of non-textured KNN is not suitable for devices. Hence, the piezoelectric coefficient of KNN has to be enhanced to match that of Pb-based materials for successful replacement. Recently, various research has been carried out on non-textured KNN ferroelectric systems to enhance the piezoelectric properties, 18 and various strategies, such as hot pressing, spark plasma sintering, microwave sintering, controlled atmosphere sintering, two-step sintering, the addition of sintering aids, and chemical modification (doping, solid solutions), have been adopted by different research groups. 7,8,19,20 The synthesis of stoichiometric KNN itself is a challenge due to the evaporation of the volatile potassium (K) and sodium (Na) at high processing temperatures, which leads to non-stoichiometry and degradation of piezoelectric properties. 15 Hence, the synthesis of highdensity KNNceramicswithprecise stoichiometry, material stability, and reproducibility under ordinary synthesis conditions is still a challenge. Therefore, KNN-based ceramics are usually prepared with a narrow processing window, that is, a small temperature range and short dwell time for sintering, to avoid the significant volatilization of alkali metal elements and to suppress abnormal grain growth (AGG). 21 It has also been established that the enhancement of the piezoelectric properties is due to the shifting of PPT to near RT. 18 However, shifting the PPT toward RT leads to narrow temperature stability of the piezoelectric properties, which can restrict its use in some applications. Thefabrication of solid solutions around the morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) is one of the suitable approaches to enhance the piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties. Lessons from the PZT, which is the solid solution of PbTiO3 and PbZrO3, suggest compositions near the MPB enhancethepiezoelectric and ferroelectric properties. This enhancement of piezoelectric properties at the MPB is due
to the flattening of free energy as a result of the easy polarization rotation pathway. 22 Another strategy to improve the piezoelectric properties of a material is by inducing local structural heterogeneity. 22,23 Using mesoscale phase field simulations, it has been reported that structural heterogeneity can further flatten the free energy profile, and enhance the piezoelectric properties. 22,23
Few reports are available on the Pb-based systems where the substitution of Sm in PMN-PT enhanced the structural heterogeneity. A high piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 ∼ 1500 pC/N) in 2.5 mol% Sm-doped Pb(Mg1/3 Nb 2/3 )O 3-PbTiO3 (PMN-PT) ceramics was reported by Li et al. The ultrahigh piezoelectricity is due to the occupancy of Sm 3 + at the A-site of PMN-PT, which produces local structural heterogeneity. 22 Kumaret al. also reported a high piezoelectric coefficient d 33 of 1160 pC/N in Sm-doped 0.71Pb(Mg1/3 Nb 2/3 )O 3 -0.29PbTiO 3 ceramics and supported the effect structural-polar heterogeneity at local scale due to the existence of different crystallographic phases. The structural heterogeneity can interact with the long-range ferroelectric; as a result, an enhanced piezoelectric property is observed. 24 Local compositional heterogeneity, in contrast, reduces the piezoelectric properties, as reported by Wang et al. on Sm-doped PMN-PT. They reported a decrease in the d 33 value for the sample with local compositional heterogeneity compared to the sample without local compositional heterogeneity. 25 Li et al. reported ultrahigh d 33 of ∼ 1500 pC/N and high dielectric permittivity of > 13,000 in Sm-doped PMN-PT ceramics. The higher values of d 33 and Ɛ r are due to local structural heterogeneity. 23 Theoretically, based on the density functional theory (DFT) calculations, it has also been seen that Sm is the most effective element for substitution to induce local structure heterogeneity in the PMN-PT system. 22
The substitution of higher valence and small-size ions (e.g., Sm 3 + ions) at the A-site changes the crystal structure and also introduces atomic disorders/local structural heterogeneity in such materials. 22 Seshadri et al. studied the temperature-dependent piezoelectric coefficient d 33 in Sm-, La-, and Nb-doped Pb1 -x Zr x TiO3 (PZT) ceramics. Among the prepared samples, the 2 mol% Sm-doped PZT shows the highest d 33 (915 pm/V) value. The highest d 33 is due to the coexistence of tetragonal and pseudo-cubic phases below T C. 26 A phase transition from antiferroelectric (AFE) P-phase to AFE R-phase has been reported by Wang et al. for 0.88Na 1 -3 x Sm x NbO3-0.12Sr0.7 Bi 0.2 TiO 3 ceramics. For x > 0.01, this ceramic shows relaxor-like behavior. 27 The photoluminescence and electrical properties of Sm-doped 0.948(K0.5 Na 0.5 NbO 3 )-0.052(LiSbO 3 ) (KNN-5.2LS) ceramics were studied by Hao et al. They have reported that Sm2 O 3 substitution into KNN-5.2LS induces a phase transition from the mixed phases of orthorhombic and tetragonal phases to a pseudo-cubic phase and shifts the PPT below the RT. The 0.4 mol% Smdoped KNN-5.2LS shows the strongest reddish-orange emission (upon blue light excitation), the highest piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 = 176 pC/N, d* 33 = 230 pm/V), and maximumsensing sensitivity (7.5 × 10 -4 Kat 293 K). 18 Sun et al. studied the photochromism, luminescence modulation, and ferroelectric energy storage properties of 1 mol% Sm-doped K0.5Na0.5 NbO3 ceramic. They have reported that the samples show a reversible color change from green to pale gray by alternating visible light irradiation ( λ > 407 nm) and thermal stimulus (230 ◦ C). 28 Sm-doped K0.5 Na 0.5 NbO3 ceramics have been prepared by Lin et al., and their optical transmittance, photochromism, photoluminescence, and PL modulation properties have been investigated. The 2 mol% Sm-doped KNN shows the highest transparency ( T ∼ 55%) at 700 nm and reversible photochromism by alternating the illumination and thermal stimulus. Sm doping in the KNN system improves sintering behavior, and a higher density ( > 95% of theoretical density) has been obtained. 28 Apart from the aforementioned enhanced piezoelectric properties, the Sm-doped KNNsystemalsoshowsnormalferroelectric behavior with improved ferroelectric properties. 29
To the best of our knowledge, very few reports systematically correlate the composition, structure, and ferroelectric/dielectric properties of the Sm-doped KNN systems. The work presented here discusses the systematic investigation of the effect of Sm doping on the physical properties and their correlation with the structural heterogeneity as well.

((K 0.5 Na0.5 ) 1 -3 x Sm x )NbO3 (KNSN), where x = 0.00, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, and 0.02 were synthesized using solid-state reaction technique. Stoichiometric amounts of high-purity carbonates of K2CO3 (99% Alfa Aesar), Na2CO3 (99.5% Sigma Aldrich), and oxides of Sm 2 O 3 (99.9% Alfa Aesar), and Nb2O5 (99.99% Sigma Aldrich) were taken as the precursors. Before weighing, the carbonates were preheated at 220 ◦ C for 4 h to remove the moisture content. The precursors were weighed for the targeted stoichiometry and then mixed and ground using an agate mortar and pestle, both in dry and in acetone medium, for about 4 h. The resulting fine-ground powders were then transferred to an alumina crucible and calcined at 875 ◦ C for 6 h in air. The calcined powders were again ground and thoroughly mixed with 3 wt% polyvinyl alcohol solution. This powder was then pressed into a cylindrical disk with a diameter of 10 mm
and a thickness of around 1 mm using a uniaxial hydraulic press. Finally, the green pellets were air-sintered at 1100 ◦ C for 3 h with a heating rate of 5 ◦ per minute for densification and used for various characterizations.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the ceramics powder were recorded using a Bruker D2-Phaser X-ray diffractometer, with Cu Kα 1 radiation ( λ = 1.5406 Å) at RT. Prior to the XRD measurement, the sintered pellets were crushed, ground into fine powder, and then sieved. In order to remove the inter-granular stress developed by the grinding process, the powders were heated at 500 ◦ C. The data was collected in Bragg's angle range of 20 ◦ ≤ 2 θ ≤ 90 ◦ with a step size of 0.02, and a scan rate of 2 ◦ /min. The RT Ramanspectroscopic measurement was performed using a micro Raman spectrometer (inVia, Renishaw). The surface morphology and microstructures of the sintered samples were analyzed by recording the micrographs using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) (JOEL Inc., #IT800). For the electrical measurements, the sintered pellets were electroded with silver paste and then dried at 200 ◦ C. The dielectric measurements were carried out over a wide frequency range (100 Hz to 1 MHz) using an LCR meter (HIOKI IM3570) in the temperature range of RT to 500 ◦ C. The polarization versus electric field ( P -E ) hysteresis loop measurement of the ceramics was carried out at RT using a ferroelectric loop tracer (Radiant Ferroelectric Tester) at 5 Hz. For the piezoelectric measurement, silver-electroded samples were first poled in a silicone oil bath around 30 kV/cm for 16 h at RT. The piezoelectric coefficient d 33 was then measured with the help of a d 33 piezometer (APC International Ltd.).

The RT XRD patterns of KNSN ceramics with various Sm content ( x = 0.00, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, and 0.02) are shown in Figure S1. For all compositions, the XRD patterns exhibit sharp, well-defined peaks, suggesting the formation of the materials with perovskite structure. However, for higher compositions (i.e., for x = 0.015 and 0.02), minor secondary peaks appear, and their intensity increases with increasing Sm concentration.
To study the effect of Sm doping on the crystal structure of KNN ceramics, we first present a qualitative interpretation of the RT XRD data of the KNSN ceramics. The

analysis is mainly based on a visual examination of the splitting of pseudo-cubic (pc) { h 00}pc , { h h 0} pc , and { h h h } pc reflections. It has been reported that all the pc reflections are singlet for cubic symmetry, whereas the { h 00}pc , { h h 0} pc , and { h h h } pc reflections are doublet for orthorhombic symmetry. On the other hand, tetragonal symmetry is characterized by the doublet nature of { h 00}pc , and { hh 0} pc reflections and the singlet nature of { hh h } pc reflections. However, for rhombohedral crystal structure, a reverse trend in the peak splitting of pc reflections is observed, that is, the { h h h } pc reflections split into doublet and the { h 00}pc and { h h 0} pc reflections are singlet. 6,9,30
Figure 1 shows the evolution of XRD profiles as a function of composition for the pc reflections {1 1 1} pc , {2 0 0} pc , {2 2 0} pc , and {2 2 2} pc of KNSN ceramics in the composition range 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.02. Due to the presence of weak distortions for the lower order reflections, here we have concentrated mainly on the {2 0 0} pc ,{2 2 0} pc , and {2 2 2} pc higher order reflections.
For pure KNN ( x = 0), the {2 0 0} pc reflection observed around 45 ◦ split into (2 0 0)/(0 2 0) in 2:1 intensity ratio. 31 Concurrently, an opposite trend in the peak splitting of the {2 2 0} pc reflection (compared to the {2 0 0} pc reflection) is observed, and the {2 2 2} pc reflection shows a doublet, which clearly suggests the orthorhombic structure. 30 For
x = 0.005, the splitting of the {2 0 0} pc , {2 2 0} pc , and {2 2 2} pc reflections are observed similar to pure KNN. However, the intensity of the (0 2 0) peak in {2 0 0} pc reflection increases as compared to the (0 2 0) peak of pure KNN, and the {2 2 0} pc and {2 2 2} pc reflections are slightly broadened. A decrease in the resolution of {2 2 0} pc and {2 2 2} pc reflections and broadening of the XRD profiles may suggest the presence of an additional phase along with the orthorhombic phase. As the Sm concentration increases, a distinct change in the shape of the profile is observed for x = 0.01 wheretheintensity of the (0 2 0) peak further increases and the (2 0 0) and (0 2 0) peaks overlap with each other. The {2 2 0} pc and {2 2 2} pc reflections also become singlet and broaden. The overlapping of the (2 0 0) and (0 2 0) peaks andsinglet nature of {2 2 0} pc and{222}pc reflections can be correlated with the presence of an additional phase along with the orthorhombic phase. 9,30 With a further increase in Sm concentration, similar behavior in the peak overlap continues for x = 0.015. The splitting of {2 0 0} pc reflection further reduces, and the profiles become more broad. This may be due to the increased fraction of the additional crystallographic phase with increasing Sm concentration. For x = 0.02, all the pc reflections become singlet, suggesting a cubic like structure. 6,9,30 The peak broadening of the pc reflections in the case of modified ferroelectric systems is usually accompanied by the coexistence of another crystallographic phase along with the parent orthorhombic phase. It has been reported by various groups that, in Sm substituted ferroelectric systems, the peak broadening is consistent with the presence of a second phase, and that creates structural heterogeneity in the system. 18,29
To ascertain the exact nature of the crystal structure quantitatively, the Rietveld refinement of the XRD data was carried out using FULLPROF software. 6,32 Here, the initial models used for the refinement were based on the information obtained from the qualitative analysis of the splitting of the XRD spectra. In the refinement process, the pseudo-Voigt function was used to model the peak shape, whereas the linear interpolation technique was used to refine the background shape. Various refined parameters, such as zero correction, scale factor, lattice parameters, Wyckoffpositions, background, and half-width parameters (U, V, and W), were refined while keeping the occupancy fixed during the refinement.
Figure 2 shows the Rietveld refined XRD patterns of KNSN ceramics at RT. For pure KNN, the XRD data was fitted with a single-phase orthorhombic structure using the Amm 2 SG, and the result shows good agreement between the experimental and fitted data (Figure 2A). Although the visual examination of the splitting of the {2 0 0} pc , {2 2 0} pc , and {2 2 2} pc reflections (into doublet) clearly suggests the orthorhombic structure for x = 0.005; however, the Rietveld refinement using single-phase

Amm 2 structure resulted in a poor fit. Thus, the Rietveld refinement for x = 0.005 was performed using various models, including (i) single-phase Amm 2, (ii) Amm 2 + P 4 mm dual phase, and (iii) Amm 2 + /u1D443/u1D45A ̄ 3/u1D45A dual phase. The Amm 2 symmetry has 12 optical modes and the irreducible representations are 4A1 + A2 + 4B1 + 3B2 according to group theory analysis. 36,37 Owing to complication of the assignment of the vibrational mode symmetries in polycrystalline ceramics, we follow the assignments of mode symmetry in [(K 0.56 Na0.44 )(Nb 0.65 Ta0.35 )O 3 , KNNT] single crystals in the present study. 36
As can be seen in Figure 3A, the Raman spectrum of the KNNceramicsinthefrequencyrangeof15-1000 cm -1 consist of primarily B 2 (TO1) ( ∼ 54 cm -1 ), B 1 (TO1) ( ∼ 73 cm -1 ), A1(TO1) ( ∼ 103 cm -1 ), A1(TO2) ( ∼ 138 cm -1 ), A1(LO1) ( ∼ 195 cm -1 ), B 1 (TO2) ( ∼ 236 cm -1 ), A 1 (TO3) ( ∼ 260 cm -1 ), A1(LO2) ( ∼ 438 cm -1 ), B2 (TO 2 ) ( ∼ 550 cm -1 ), A1(TO4) ( ∼ 612 cm -1 ), and A1(LO3) ( ∼ 860 cm -1 ) as shown in Figure 3A-C and in Figure S2. It is observed that A1(TO3), B2 (TO 2 ), A1(TO4), and A1(LO3) each modes splits into two modes marked as A1(TO3)1( ∼ 256 cm -1 ) and A1(TO3)2 ( ∼ 271 cm -1 ), B2 (TO 2 ) 1 ( ∼ 546 cm -1 ) and B2 (TO 2 ) 2 ( ∼ 564 cm -1 ), A1(TO4)1 ( ∼ 594 cm -1 ) and A1(TO4)2 ( ∼ 617 cm -1 ), and A1(LO3)1 ( ∼ 857 cm -1 ) and A1(LO3)2 ( ∼ 873 cm -1 ), respectively. The splitting of Raman modes may be due to the various local order regions in KNN ceramics. 38 The observed Raman active modes indicate the orthorhombic phase of the KNN ceramics, 36,37 which is backed by XRD and dielectric results (below). Notethat the B 2 (TO 1 ) mode vanishes at x = 0.010, as shown in Figure 3B,C. The disappearance of the B 2 (TO 1 ) mode indicates the structural transition of the KNSN ceramics. It is significant that an overdamped mode emerges at about 72 cm -1 at x = 0.010 (Figure 3B), corresponding to the E(TO1 ) mode of the tetragonal phase of the KNSN ceramics. 39 Therefore, the disappearance of B 2 (TO 1 ) mode and the emergence of an overdamped E(TO1 ) mode imply the structural transition from the orthorhombic to the tetragonal phase of the KNSN ceramics. It is important to note that the splitting of the B2 (TO 2 ) persists in the KNSN (0.010 ≤ x ≤ 0.02) ceramics. The persistence of the B2 (TO 2 ) mode splitting may imply the phase coexistence of orthorhombic ( Amm 2) and tetragonal ( P 4 mm ) phases in KNSN (0.010 ≤ x ≤ 0.02) ceramics. The Rietveld refinement of the XRD spectra agrees with the coexistence of orthorhombic ( Amm 2) and tetragonal ( P 4 mm ) phases KNSN (0.005 ≤ x ≤ 0.02). 39

The near-perfect NbO6 octahedron of pure KNN ( x = 0) belongs to Amm 2 symmetry is seen by the intense ν 1 and ν 5 modes. 37 It is found that the frequency ( ∼ 54 cm -1 ) of B 2 (TO1 ) modes associated to A-site cations shifts to a lower frequency of 45 cm -1 with the Sm doping ( x = 0.005). This result
suggests that the substitution of heavier Sm ions with lighter K/Na ions confirms the A-site occupancy of the Sm ions in KNSN ceramics.
To comprehend the Sm-doping effects on local heterogeneities in KNSN ceramics, the CP, which is associated with the relaxation process of polar clusters or PNRs, 40 has been investigated as a function of composition. The observed soft mode phenomena imply a displacive phase transition, whereas the existence of the CP denotes an order-disorder phase transition of either a crystal or a ceramic. In an orthorhombic phase of pure KNN ceramic, the low-frequency B 2 (TO 1 ) mode is seen at about 54 cm -1 , whereas the overdamped E(TO1 ) mode at around 72 cm -1 is observed in the mixed (orthorhombic + tetragonal) phases of the KNSN (0.010 ≤ x ≤ 0.020) in the present study. Without temperature-dependent Raman scattering results, it is difficult to opine about the soft-mode nature of the B 2 (TO1) and E(TO1 ) modes. Hence, the order-disorder nature of ferroelectric phase transition is found due to the existence of prominent CP in KNSN ceramics. 34,35,40 It is well established that the dynamic PNRs begin to appear in the paraelectric phase at the so-called Burns temperature ( T B ). 41 These PNRs become static at an intermediate temperature ( T *). 34,35 Due to the local polarization freezing in the ferroelectric phase, these static PNRs transform into randomly oriented nano-domain states and convert them into macro-domain states. 42,43 Note that in the lower part in Figure 3C, the Γ CP , which is associated with the relaxation process of fluctuating local polar clusters, 34,35,40 decreases at x = 0.005, then increases with Sm-doping, and almost constant (slightly scattered) in the range of 0.010 ≤ x ≤ 0.020 of the KNSN ceramics. With increasing Sm composition in the same structural phase, the correlation among nano-domain states may be bolstered owing to the increase of number density and/or size of randomly oriented nano-domain states, resulting in a decrease in the value of the Γ CP. 6,39,44 Theanomalous change of the Γ CP in KNSN ( x = 0.010) indicates the structural phase transition of KNSN ceramics. In the range of 0.010 ≤ x ≤ 0.020, the value of Γ CP is almost constant (Figure 3C), where KNSN belongs to (orthorhombic + tetragonal) phases. These findings indicate that the correlation among nano-domain states may be weak and/or broken giving rise to the almost constant fluctuations of domain wall motion because of the coexistence of phases. 6,39

The presence of nanoscale structural heterogeneity can disrupt the formation of long-range order ferroelectric domain, which leads to the appearance of relaxation behavior at T O-T . In the ferroelectric phase of KNSN, the presence of local structural heterogeneity is observed by composition-dependent CP and dielectric behavior, whereas the phase boundary (i.e., coexistence of orthorhombic and tetragonal phases) is found by the analysis of XRD spectra. Hence, Sm 3 + substitutions create inter-ferroelectric phase boundary (i.e., coexistence of orthorhombic and tetragonal phases as observed from XRD) and induce structural heterogeneity so that both of these phenomena cooperatively help the formation of relaxation behavior at T O-T of the KNSN. As the Sm concentration increased further, similar behavior of the phase transition peaks continued for all the compositions. A similar observation has also been reported in multicomponent substituted KNN system. 47 Further, the temperature dependence of Ɛ r for the ceramics measured at 10 kHz with different Sm content is shown in Figure 5F, whereas the inset figure shows the Ɛ r versus T plot for pure KNN. The compositional-driven structural phase transition takes place in ferroelectric solid solutions. 23 When the composition approaches the MPB, an exceptional increase in the dielectric, ferroelectric, ferroelastic, and piezoelectric properties are obtained due to the flattening of the free energy profile. 23 So, the general guiding principle to increase the piezoelectric properties is the construction of MPBinferroelectric solid solutions. 23,25 This approach has been well verified by various research groups. 23,25 However, there is a limit on the flattening of the free energy profile as the compositional driven phase transition is a first-order phase transition. 23 Thus, further enhancement of the piezoelectric properties above a critical value has not beenobtainedincaseoftheMPB.However,ithasalsobeen reported that the critical volume fraction of the local structural heterogeneity creates higher interfacial energy due to the small size with higher specific area as compared to the KNN matrix. So the nanoscale structural heterogeneity effectively creates interfacial energy and the competition between interfacial energy and bulk energy may need further flattening of the free energy profile and result in an enhancement of piezoelectric properties. 25
Based on the detailed literature survey, two important questions arise: (i) does structural heterogeneity play an important role in the enhancement of the piezoelectric properties for ferroelectric systems? (ii) is structural heterogeneity limited to only Pb-based relaxor (such as PMN-PT and PZT) ferroelectric systems for enhanced piezoelectric response?. 49 To understand these questions, we have systematically studied the effect of Sm on KNN.
It has been reported that the enhancement of piezoelectric properties in case of KNN system sometimes associated with the homogeneous distribution of grains with better microstructure. 18 Here, the grain size of x = 0.05% Sm is similar to the pure KNN ( x = 0), so the change in the piezoelectric properties is not associated with the grain size and microstructure of the Sm-doped KNN system. It has also been presented in Section 1 that the shifting of the T O-T toward RT is one of the well-accepted approaches to increase the piezoelectric coefficient. 18 As there is a small increase in the T O-T value and T C values are nearly unaffected with substitution of Sm in KNN-Sm system, so the enhancement of dielectric and piezoelectric properties is
not associated with the change in the phase transition temperature. So we expect the enhancement of dielectric and piezoelectric properties to be associated with the increase in the degree of structural heterogeneity and induction of relaxation behavior at T O-T phase transition temperature. The linear variation of dielectric constant with frequency allows us to find the slope, and the relative change in the magnitude of the slope can be used as the (qualitative) measure of the structural heterogeneity present in the system. 49 It has been observed from Figure S5 that structural heterogeneity parameter increases for x = 0.05% Sm (which is a maximum for the present study) compared to pure KNN ( x = 0.0), and after that, it decreases. So, the change in the structural heterogeneity is associated with a change in Sm concentration in KNSN ceramics. The maximum structural heterogeneity is observed for a critical concentration of the tetragonal phase where the maximum piezoelectric coefficient is obtained. However, the piezoelectric coefficient decreases with further increase in the Sm concentrations. The decrease in the piezoelectric properties above the critical concentration may be due to the dominant contribution of the tetragonal phase, which prevents the stabilization of a long-range ferroelectric phase. The induction of the tetragonal ( P 4 mm ) phase in the parent orthorhombic ( Amm 2) phase due to the Sm-substitutions increases the structural disorder, which has been reflected in terms of broadening of the pc reflections (Figure 1). The fraction of the tetragonal phases also increases with the increase in the Sm concentrations (Table S1). The tetragonal ( P 4 mm ) phase can be incorporated with the parent Amm 2 phase to account for the local structural heterogeneity. 24 The structural heterogeneity/disorder induced by tetragonal ( P 4 mm ) phase maynot be compatible with long-range ferroelectric ordering of orthorhombic ( Amm 2) phase; therefore, it breaks the long-range ferroelectric ordering above the optimal concentration. As a result, a decrease in the ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties is observed above the critical concentration. 50 Similar explanations have also been reported for Sm-doped PMN-PT system by Kumar et al. 24
conclusion:
In summary, high-density KNSN ceramics were successfully fabricated by the conventional solid-state reaction route. The phase transition behavior, surface morphology, dielectric, ferroelectric, and piezoelectric properties have been systematically investigated over various experimental conditions. The XRD and Raman data confirmed a compositional-driven structural phase transition from orthorhombic ( Amm 2) phase to the orthorhombic + tetragonal ( Amm 2 + P 4 mm ) dual phase with an
increase in Sm concentration at RT. The temperaturedependent dielectric properties show two phase transitions, orthorhombic to tetragonal ( T O-T ) and tetragonal to cubic phase transition ( T C), for all the compositions. Unlike ferroelectric to paraelectric phase transition, the T O-T transitions manifest as relaxation behavior in the dielectric constant and loss peak in Sm-modified KNN systems. The induction of structural heterogeneity at the inter-ferroelectric phase boundary in Sm-modified KNN systems is the origin of the appearance of the relaxation behavior. With the increase in Sm concentration, the T O-T slightly increases, whereas T C value remains constant, though broadening of the peak at the phase transition occurs with increasing Sm. The dielectric constant at RT increases initially with Sm concentration, goes through a maximum for x = 0.005, and decreases after that. Among the prepared samples of (K0.5 Na 0.5 ) 1 -3 x Sm x )NbO3, the ceramic with x = 0.005 has the optimum ferroelectric properties and maximum piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 = 94 pC/N). The rise in the degree of local structural heterogeneity due to Sm doping is the reason for the enhanced piezoelectric properties of ((K 0.5 Na0.5 ) 1 -3 x Sm x )NbO3 ceramics with critical composition x = 0.005.

article_title: High-Performance Lead-Free Ceramics With Simultaneously High Piezoelectricity and High Mechanical Quality Factor
abstract: Piezoelectric materials with a high piezoelectric coefficient (d33) and high mechanical quality factor (Qm) are vital for advanced high‐power applications. However, achieving this combination is challenging, particularly for lead‐free piezoelectrics, because a high d33 value relies on mobile domain walls, which increase dissipative losses and reduce Qm. In this study, this longstanding trade‐off is overcome by introducing defect dipoles (via Mn doping) into the quadruple point (QP) composition of the lead‐free Ba(Sn, Ti)O3 system. The resultant 0.5%Mn‐doped Ba(Sn0.11Ti0.89)O3 (BST‐0.5%Mn) ceramic exhibits a high d33 value of 710 pC/N and high Qm value of 929, while the BST‐1%Mn ceramic achieves a d33 value of 614 pC/N and Qm value of 1138. These values represent a 10‐fold increase in Qm and 1.6‐fold increase in d33 for BST‐0.5%Mn, compared to those for undoped BST. High‐resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy and phase‐field simulations reveal that the enhanced d33 and Qm are attributable to the coexistence of multiple phases of QPs with symmetry‐conforming defect dipoles, challenging the long‐held notion of physical incompatibility between high d33 and high Qm. These findings offer a pathway for designing eco‐friendly piezoelectric materials with unprecedented performance, paving the way for sustainable and efficient high‐power applications.

Sample Preparation : Ba((Sn 0.11 Ti 0.89 ) 1x Mn x )O 3 ( x = 0, 0.25%, 0.5%, 1%, and 2%) (abbreviated as BSTx Mn) ceramics were synthesized using conventional solid-state reaction method. High-purity raw chemicals including BaCO 3 (99.8%), TiO 2 (99.8%), SnO 2 (99.9%), and MnO 2 (99.99%) were accurately weighed according to the stoichiometry of the desired compositions. The mixture was then ball milled using yttriastabilized zirconia media in ethanol solvent for 12 h to obtain a homogeneous powder mixture. Subsequently, the dried powder was calcined at 1300 ° C for 4 h and subjected to an additional 12 h ball-milling step. The obtained powder was dried and pressed into pellets with a diameter of 8 mm and a thickness of 1.5 mm using a cold isostatic press at a pressure of 200 MPa. The sintering process was carried out in air at 1425 ° C for 4 h. Following sintering, silver paste electrodes were applied to the ceramic pellets and then fired at 700 ° C for 30 min to ensure proper adhesion. Subsequently, electric poling was performed by subjecting the samples to a direct current field of 2 kV mm -1 for 30 min in a silicone oil bath.

[2a,c,d,6,7] Compared to known piezoelectric ceramics, lead-free BSTx Mn ceramics simultaneously exhibit exceptionally high d 33 and Q m values, overcoming the trade-o/uniFB00 between high d 33 and high Q m.
Figures S1 and S2 (Supporting Information) shows the X-ray di/uniFB00raction (XRD) patterns and scanning electron microscopy micrographs of the di/uniFB00erent ceramics, indicating that all samples display typical perovskite and dense structures. Figure 2 a shows the variation in the dielectric constant with temperature during cooling at 10 3 Hz for the di/uniFB00erent ceramics. Among them, the BST-0Mn ceramic exhibits the highest dielectric permittivity of 54 400 at the Curie temperature ( T C ). As the Mn content increases, the dielectric permittivity at T C decreases. Figure 2b shows the impedance and phase angle of the di/uniFB00erent components as a function of frequency. The BST-0.5%Mn and BST1%Mn samples exhibit higher phase angles, indicating a better

The uniaxial strain curves of di/uniFB00erent components under a low electric field of 2 kV/cm are shown in Figure 2c. The BST-0Mn ceramic exhibits a high strain of 0.034%, while the BST-0.5%Mn ceramic exhibits a strain of 0.0175%. The corresponding piezoelectric strain coe/uniFB03cient, S max / E max ( d 33 * ), of the QP BST-0Mn composition is 1700 pm/V, which is higher than the value reported by Li et al. for Sm-PMN-29PT (2.5%Smdoped 71%Pb(Mg1/3 Nb 2/3 )O3 -29%PbTiO3 ) ceramics. [9] The BST0.5%Mn composition exhibits a d 33 * value of 875 pm/V. In contrast, the piezoelectric coe/uniFB03cient d 33 of BST-0Mn is 433 pC/N. The d 33 values of BST-0.5%Mn and BST-1%Mn are 710 and 614 pC/N, respectively. The large di/uniFB00erence between d 33 * and d 33 of the BST-0Mn ceramic is due to the non-ideal poling state, as described below.
Figure 2d provides a comprehensive comparison of d 33 , Q m, and ɛ r (at room temperature, 21 ° C) for the BST-0Mn, BST0.5%Mn, and BST-1%Mn ceramics. It is evident that the performance of the Mn-doped samples is significantly improved. The BST-0.5%Mn ceramic simultaneously possesses high d 33, Q m , ɛ r values of 710 pC/N, 929, and 36 500, respectively. Likewise, the BST-%1Mn sample has high d 33, Q m , and ɛ r values of 614 pC/N, 1138, and 33 200, respectively. Compared to those of the undoped BST ceramic, the Q m and d 33 values of the BST-0.5%Mn sample increase by 10 and 1.6 times, respectively, and the Q m and d 33 values of the BST-1%Mn sample increase by 12 and 1.4 times, respectively.
Figure 3 presents the polarization-electric field ( P -E ) hysteresis loops under a low electric field and the bipolar strain-electric field ( S -E ) curves under a high electric field for the poled and aged BSTx Mnsamples, as well as the variation in the maximum polarization P m, remnant polarization P r , internal bias field E i , maximum strain S m, and the corresponding hysteresis as a function of the Mn doping content. As the Mn content increases, the P m, P r , and S m contents of the samples gradually decrease. While E i increases significantly with the increase of Mn content, indicating that the pinning e/uniFB00ect of the samples is enhanced. This phenomenon is related to the increased oxygen vacancy in the samples with higher Mn doping content (see Supplementary Material, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy results, Figure S6, Supporting Information). Concurrently, as the Mn content increases, the area enclosed by the P -E hysteresis loops decreases continuously. The decrease in the area of the P -E loop corresponds to a decrease in the energy dissipation associated with domain switching and domain wall motion under an electric field. The incorporation of Mn is known to enhance domain wall pinning, restricting its mobility under alternating electric fields. Lower energy dissipation intrinsically implies a higher probability of achieving a high Q m in these materials. Therefore, the area of the P -E loops measured under low-field conditions after poling and aging can, to a certain extent, be used as an indicator for evaluating the relative magnitude of Q m in these piezoelectric ceramics.

The high d 33 values observed for the Mn-doped QP compositions in this work originate from the coexistence of multiple phases of QPs with symmetry-conforming defect dipoles. According to the Landau phenomenological theory, a high d 33 can be obtained via flattening of the Gibbs free-energy density profile with respect to polarization. [ 15] QP composition presents a coexistence of multiple phases (C, T, O, R), where the polarization rotation energy barrier nearly vanishes (Figure S9, Supporting Information), [12b,c,15c] theoretically leading to high dielectric and piezoelectric properties. Consequently, in ferroelectric systems with QP, QP composition usually exhibits the highest dielectric constant at T C . [ 15c,16] However, owing to the coexistence of multiphase structures with extremely small domain sizes of QP composition in this work, the unpoled QP samples are prone to depolarization after poling. In other words, after the poling process, some domains cannot maintain their alignment along the electric field direction during the aging process, resulting in random domain orientation. The undoped QP composition with a non-ideal poling state can be demonstrated by the frequency-dependent phase angle of the planar vibration mode curves (Figure 2b). It is widely recognized that the maximum phase angle ( /u1D703 max ) is closely associated with the poling degree. The BST-0Mn sample shows a low /u1D703 max of ≈ 70 ° , indicating a nonideal poling state. [ 1d,8,17] This explains why the BST-0Mn composition fails to exhibit a theoretically high piezoelectric coe/uniFB03cient and instead shows only a moderate d 33 value. Whereas, the potential for high piezoelectric property of the undoped QP composition can be confirmed by measuring its d 33 * value under a low electric field. As shown in Figure 2c, the undoped BST QP composition demonstrates the highest d 33 * value (approaching 1700 pm/V), which is consistent with the phase-field simulation results in Figure 5d. Therefore, if the depolarization e/uniFB00ect in the QP compositions can be mitigated to maintain better poling states, the piezoelectric coe/uniFB03cient of the material can reach significantly higher values.
As a result, a key innovation of this work lies in the introduction of defect dipoles into QP compositions, where the defect dipoles e/uniFB00ectively reduce the depolarization e/uniFB00ect through the pinning e/uniFB00ect, thereby achieving increased piezoelectric coe/uniFB03cients. In the poled and aged Mn-doped samples, the defect dipoles provide defect polarization ( P D ) and internal bias field ( E i ) along the poling field direction, enabling more domains to maintain their polarization direction alignment with the poling electric field direction. The better poling state of Mn-doped BST samples can also be evidenced by the frequency-dependent phase angle curves (Figure 2b), where /u1D703 max is ≈ 83 ° , much higher than that of the BST-0Mn ceramic. [1d,8,17] In general, the ideal poling state can ensure that the piezoelectric ceramics reach their inherent maximum Q m and d 33 with the /u1D703 max nearly 90 ° . [ 1d] Further increasing the /u1D703 max of BST-0.5%Mn and BST-1%Mn samples by controlling poling treatment may further increase their Q m and d 33 . [ 1d] As a result, although the pinning e/uniFB00ect of the defect dipoles in Mn-doped BST samples may slightly reduce d 33 , the substantial improvement of the poling state leads to a net increase in d 33 . Consequently, in the BSTx Mn system, the acceptor-doped QP samples demonstrate significantly increased d 33 and Q m compared to the undoped QP compositions.
Although the model materials developed in this work exhibit low Curie temperatures, they remain viable for practical appli-
www.advmat.de cations through strategic implementation. Specifically, integrating these materials into a thermostatic system ensures optimal performance, independent of external temperature fluctuations, thereby expanding their applicability. This approach has historical precedent, such as in the 1990s, when piezoelectric materials were integrated into thermostatic systems (25 ° C) for calibrating the mirrors of the Hubble Space Telescope.
conclusion: A long-sought combinationd 33 of 710 pC/N, Q m of 929, and ɛ r of 36500-is achieved in lead-free Mn-doped Ba(Sn 0.11 Ti 0.89 )O3 (denoted as BSTx Mn) piezoelectric ceramics. These properties outperform the d 33 , Q m, and ɛ r values of existing lead-based and lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. Compared to those of the undoped QP composition (Ba(Sn 11 Ti 89 )O3 (BST)), the Q m value of the 0.5%Mn-doped BST sample increases by ∼ 1000% and its d 33 increases by ∼ 160%; the Q m of the 1%Mn-doped BST sample increases by ∼ 1200% and its d 33 increases by ∼ 140%. STEM microstructural observations and phase-field simulations indicate that the increased d 33 and Q m values are attributable to the coexistence of multiple phases of QPs with symmetry-conforming defect dipoles. Our work provides a new approach for designing piezoelectrics with simultaneously high piezoelectricity and high mechanical quality factor, which will find important applications in high-power piezoelectrics.
